steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Open files: find the entry square. This part covers When it fails; Set it up, prevent it, test it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Four things a defender can try [I].** Cover the entry square with a piece. Put a rook on the file and offer a trade. Take the file first: the mirror board below is the same road seen from the other side. Or ignore the file and threaten something bigger; we show no board for that one here. [H] I suspect club players lose more games by landing on a covered square than by arriving late; we have no count. The next boards show the first two.

steps.prompt: Think of an open file in one of your own games: who landed first, and which square did the rook want? No game to hand? Use the Carlsen game below and say who arrived first and why. [H] The player who arrived second may often believe they were first; this is untested.

steps.caption: The same position as before, with one change: the bishop stands on f5 instead of e5. White to move. Does the bishop attack d7?

line.say: The bishop captures the rook, and nothing recaptures. The entry square was guarded.

line.say: Black puts a rook opposite White's. A landing on d7 now runs into the rook on d8.
White trades. The file is now empty of rooks.
The bishop recaptures. Neither side has gained the file.

claims.statement: Contesting the file is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
The position is about equal (depth 16).

steps.caption: The same road, seen from the other side: Black takes the file first, and no white piece watches d2. White's pawns on c2 and e3 guard d3 and d4, not d2.

line.say: Black's rook lands on d2 and attacks the pawns on c2 and f2.
White defends the pawn on c2 with a rook, which also guards the first rank.
The second black rook joins the first. White's rook on c1 holds the balance, so the landing gains little here [I].

From d2 the rook attacks the pawn on c2.
From d2 the rook attacks the pawn on f2.
Landing on d2 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.text: **Opening the road, being first.** Files open by trades: a pawn exchange, or a capture that removes the pawn. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*) advises being the side that puts rooks on the file first [S]. Znosko-Borovsky adds a question to ask before opening any line: who benefits? As a rule, opening a line tends to help the stronger side, or the side with the stronger part of the position [S]. A rule of thumb, not a law.
steps.chapter: Set it up, prevent it, test it

steps.title: Same pawn, one change
steps.prompt: Black's b-pawn stands on b7 instead of b6, so it protects c6. Does the knight capture still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.

steps.caption: The Slav Defence, move four. Every file still holds a pawn, so no file is open. A pawn trade on d5 changes that. Follow the trade and ask which file opens.

line.say: White captures on d5 with the c-pawn. The white pawn has left the c-file.
Black recaptures with the c-pawn. Now neither side has a pawn on the c-file: it is open.

claims.statement: Before the trade no file is open or half-open.
After the trade the c-file is open and every other file is closed.

steps.caption: A real game: Carlsen against Vachier-Lagrave. Black's c-pawn and White's c-pawn face each other. Watch the pawn trade open the c-file.

line.say: Black captures the pawn on d4 with the c-pawn. One of the two c-file pawns leaves the file.
White recaptures with the c-pawn. The c-file now holds no pawns at all.

claims.statement: After the two captures the c-file is open.

steps.text: **A pawn on the road.** Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) separates a *protected* blocker from an unprotected one [S]. Undermine a protected one with a pawn lever. Besiege an unprotected one: bring more attackers than it has defenders, and capture with the cheapest piece first, so you give up the least if the exchange goes on. Sacrifices to clear the file come last.

steps.caption: A pawn blocks the c-file: the pawn on c6, protected by the pawn on b7. A rook cannot take it. A pawn lever can attack it. White to move. The engine sees the position as about level either way (depth 16).

line.say: The lever attacks the blocker. Black may also decline with ...c5: the lever only gains the file if Black takes [H].
Black takes the lever pawn. The blocker has left the file: the c-file is now open for both rooks.

claims.statement: The pawn on c6 is protected by the pawn on b7.
The c-file is half-open for White: no white pawn, one black pawn.
The only pawn move that attacks c6 is the lever b4-b5.
If Black takes the lever pawn, the c-file is open (the a-file and the d-file hold no pawns either).
If Black answers ...c5 instead, a black pawn still stands on the c-file: it is half-open for White, not open.
The engine rates the position as about equal (depth 16).

steps.text: **Half-open: pressure on one pawn [I].** A file where your own pawn is gone but theirs still stands is half-open for you. The rook cannot pass the blocker, but it points at it and ties defenders to it. Add attackers until they outnumber the defenders, then take.

steps.caption: The c-file is half-open for White and the pawn on c6 has no pawn protection: two attackers (rook and knight), one defender (the bishop). Which piece should take first?

line.say: The knight takes first: it is the cheapest attacker.
The bishop, the only defender, recaptures.
The rook takes the bishop. White gave a knight for a pawn and a bishop.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack c6: the rook and the knight.
One black piece, the bishop, defends c6.
The c-file is half-open for White.
Knight takes on c6 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
Taking with the rook first is worse than the knight capture by at least a pawn (depth 16).
The knight capture wins at least a pawn along the engine line.

steps.caption: Not every file is open. The d-file is closed by a white pawn and a black pawn. Two files are open: which one does the rook belong on? White to move.

line.say: The rook uses the open c-file. No black piece attacks c7, and the closed d-file never mattered.

claims.statement: The c-file and the e-file are open; the d-file is closed.
No black piece attacks c7.
Landing on c7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.text: **Remember.** A rook on an open file needs a safe entry square. A defender can cover that square or offer a rook trade, so check who watches it. Files open by trades, and being first to the file helps. If a pawn blocks the file, attack it with more pieces than defend it, cheapest piece first.
